title: Why Has Workday Stock Trailed Cadence?

Why Has Workday Stock Trailed Cadence?

Two software companies grew their sales at about the same pace over the last three years. Yet over the five years to November 2026, one stock fell 35.2% while the other gained 84.5%. The stock that fell belongs to Workday (WDAY), which sells HR and finance software, and the stock that rose belongs to Cadence Design Systems (CDNS). So where did Cadence's lead come from: faster sales growth, bigger profits, or investors paying more?

Who Has Beaten Workday Over Five Years?

Over five years, Workday's stock held up better than most of its industry, outpacing 60.8% of the 125 application software companies compared.

Still, five companies with similar sales growth, each worth at least $2 billion, beat Workday by 20 points or more over five years. Cadence was one of them, finishing ahead by 119.7 points over five years. The table below places Workday beside two of these peers.

Agilysys (AGYS), which sells software to the hospitality industry, is further ahead still, by 175.8 points, so Cadence is not the only company with similar sales growth to beat Workday.

Did Cadence Grow Faster Than Workday?

Only a little, and not over five years. Over the last three years, Cadence grew its sales about 1.3 points a year faster than Workday, putting the two companies at nearly the same pace. Between 2021 and 2026, Workday's revenue rose 117.3%, compared with 106.1% for Cadence.

Cadence sells software, hardware and design blocks that companies use to design and verify chips. Even though the two companies sell very different things, their sales grew at a similar rate, meaning faster growth does not explain Cadence's lead.

Where Did The Gap Come From?

The gap came from what investors pay, not from profits. Between 2021 and 2026, Workday moved from an operating loss to an operating profit, marking a 14.7-point swing in operating margin. This compared with a 3.5-point gain for Cadence. Over those years, Cadence's profit per share rose 102.8%, running about in step with its sales.

Because Workday had no profit in 2021, the fair yardstick for both companies is what investors paid for each dollar of sales. In 2021, those figures were close to each other: 12.6 times for Workday and 13.9 times for Cadence.

Workday's sales multiple fell 76.6% between June 2021 and June 2026, while Cadence's rose 6.0% between September 2021 and September 2026. Those dates differ from the end date of the stock returns, so the two sets of figures do not line up exactly. Workday's business became more profitable, yet by 2026 you paid far less for each dollar of Workday's sales.

title: Steve Eisman: Oracle Could Suffer if OpenAI 'Demise' Causes US Recession

Steve Eisman, famous for betting against the housing market before the 2008 crash, sees a 70% chance the AI boom ends in a bear market or worse.

He sees two ways it could go wrong: AI succeeds while investors lose money, or the technology fails to live up to its hype.

In the latest episode of The Real Eisman Playbook, he assigns 40% odds to a bear market caused by excessive investment despite AI's success. Another 30% goes to a scenario where AI proves overhyped, triggering a market crash and U.S. recession.

30% goes to the bull case.

Eisman compares AI to the railroads and early internet, technologies that transformed the world while leaving a trail of bankruptcies.

Why AI Could Succeed and Stocks Still Crash

Eisman cited expectations that technology giants will spend roughly $850 billion on AI infrastructure this year. He also pointed to research suggesting US data center capacity could reach twice actual demand by late 2027.

"There is simply way too much capex chasing demand," he said of his 40% scenario.

Competition adds another threat. Eisman argues OpenAI and Anthropic have little protection against cheaper Chinese models, leaving customers free to switch providers.

Their models are superior, he conceded, but "you don't need a Mercedes-Benz for every trip."

What Happens if the Money Stops?

Oracle Corp. (NYSE:ORCL) reported $664 billion in contracted backlog in September. Roughly half is tied to OpenAI, Eisman said, potentially exposing Oracle if the developer struggles.

Banks are also growing more cautious about financing AI infrastructure, Reuters reported Monday.

OpenAI's June-quarter revenue grew 18% from the March quarter to $6.7 billion, while its operating loss widened by $3 billion to $12.3 billion. Anthropic's revenue more than doubled to $11.6 billion over the same period, The Wall Street Journal reported.

"I'm starting to think that the demise of OpenAI would push the U.S. into an immediate recession," Eisman said.

He stressed, however, that he isn't predicting OpenAI will fail.

What Prediction Markets Say

Traders on Polymarket gave an AI bubble burst roughly 6% odds by December 2026 and around 23% by June 2027 on Tuesday. The contract requires three severe events within 90 days, such as major chip-stock declines or an AI developer's bankruptcy, so a milder bear market like Eisman's 40% scenario might not trigger it.

Traders also appear to share Eisman's doubts about OpenAI. Polymarket gives Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOGL) roughly 71% odds of having the top-ranked AI model at year-end, compared with 21% for Anthropic and just 2.5% for OpenAI.

Intel (INTC) plunged 43% in a month after guiding Q4 earnings per share to $0.25 from $0.52 as PC weakness drags into 2027.

Data center revenue jumped 78% to $7 billion, and Intel expects supply constraints through 2027, with Oracle and NVIDIA wins backing demand.

The CFO says 2027 is "probably not a dynamic where we're going to have positive free cash flow," leaving a 33x forward P/E exposed.

Intel (NASDAQ:INTC) trades at $59.37. The stock has fallen 43.3% in a month after management laid out a weak fourth-quarter outlook, so investors need to decide how much of that bad news the price already reflects.

Coolcaesar / Wikimedia Commons

Intel sells Xeon server chips through its Data Center and AI (DCAI) unit and Core Ultra PC processors through its client group. It also runs Intel Foundry, which makes chips for Intel and for outside customers. The shares rose from $48.26 at the January earnings report to $103.79 by July. Then came the Q3 outlook. Management guided Q4 revenue to $15.0B to $16.0B, below Q3's $16.51B. It guided non-GAAP EPS to $0.25, down from $0.52, and said the PC slowdown should last at least through the first half of 2027.

Server Demand Is Running Ahead of Intel's Supply

The bulls point to data center demand. DCAI revenue rose 78% to $7.32B, and the unit's operating income reached $3.04B. Management expects DCAI to grow by a mid-teens percentage sequentially in Q4 and sees the industry staying "supply-constrained throughout 2027 and into 2028." The CEO said agentic AI workloads could take the server CPU market "from $40 billion to more than $200 billion over five years."
